text: Park Geun-hye, born on 2 February 1952 in Samdeok-dong, Jung District, Daegu, South Korea, is a South Korean politician who served as the 11th president of South Korea from 25 February 2013 until her removal from office in 2017. She is the eldest daughter of Park Chung Hee, who became the third president of South Korea after the May 16 military coup in 1961 and served from 1963 to 1979, and his wife, First Lady Yuk Young-soo. Both of her parents were assassinated; her mother, Yuk Young-soo, was killed on 15 August 1974 in the National Theater of Korea during an assassination attempt by Mun Se-gwang, and her father, Park Chung Hee, was assassinated on 26 October 1979 by his intelligence chief, Kim Jae-gyu. Park Geun-hye served as the first lady of South Korea from 1974 until her father's assassination. She has a younger sister, Park Geun-ryeong, a younger brother, Park Ji-man, and an older half-sister, Park Jae-ok. She is unmarried and has no children. Park graduated from Sogang University in 1974 with a bachelor's degree in electronic engineering and briefly studied at Joseph Fourier University in France before leaving after her mother's murder. She received honorary doctoral degrees from the Chinese Culture University in Taiwan in 1987, Pukyong National University and KAIST in 2008, Sogang University in 2010, and TU Dresden in 2014. Park served as a member of the National Assembly for four consecutive terms between 1998 and 2012, first elected in a 1998 by-election for Dalseong County (Daegu), and was re-elected three times in the same district until April 2012. In 2012, she announced she would not run for a constituency seat but instead for a proportional representative position to lead the Saenuri Party, which she won in the April 2012 election. She was leader of the conservative Grand National Party (GNP) from 2004 to 2006 and later the Liberty Korea Party (Saenuri Party) from 2011 to 2012. In 2006, she was attacked by Ji Chung-ho, who slashed her face with a utility knife, causing an 11-centimeter wound requiring 60 stitches; after recovery, she reportedly said, "How is Daejeon?" which contributed to the victory of the GNP candidate in the Daejeon mayoral race. She earned the nickname "Queen of Elections" for leading the GNP to win all 40 reelections and by-elections during her tenure as chairwoman from 2004 to 2006. In 2007, she visited Harvard University, where she advocated for a stronger U.S.-South Korea relationship. She was the leading candidate for the 2012 presidential election in every national poll between 2008 and September 2011, with approval ratings ranging from 25% to 45%, and was the top candidate in a national survey with a 45.5% approval rating in August 2012 and a 50.6% rating in a two-way competition against Ahn Cheol-soo in September. She was elected president on 19 December 2012 with 51.6% of the vote. Her inauguration on 25 February 2013, the largest in South Korean history with 70,000 participants, included diplomatic representatives from 24 countries. In her inauguration speech, she outlined a vision of "a new era of hope and happiness" with five administrative goals: a jobs-centered creative economy, tailored employment and welfare, creativity-oriented education and cultural enrichment, a safe and united society, and strong security measures for peace on the Korean Peninsula. She emphasized economic prosperity, people's happiness, cultural enrichment, and peaceful unification. She restructured the Blue House and government, launching new offices including the Office of National Security, the Ministry of Science, ICT and Future Planning, and the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, and revived the Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs. On 5 June 2013, she announced a plan to build a "Creative Economy" to revitalize the economy and create jobs. In April 2013, she emphasized the importance of timely economic policy and encouraged the gig economy. On 8 April 2014, she signed the Australia–Korea Free Trade Agreement with Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott. Park proposed eliminating the "Four Major Social Evils"—sexual violence, domestic violence, school violence, and unsafe food—and launched the National Unity Committee on 17 June 2013, chaired by Han Kwang-ok, to resolve societal conflicts and promote co-existence. After taking office, she met with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and President Barack Obama, and made her first foreign trip to the United States in May 2013. In 2017, the National Intelligence Service admitted it had conducted an illicit campaign to influence the 2012 presidential election to ensure Park defeated Moon Jae-in. In 2016, Park was impeached by the National Assembly on charges of influence peddling by her aide, Choi Soon-sil, and Prime Minister Hwang Kyo-ahn assumed her duties as acting president. The Constitutional Court upheld the impeachment on 10 March 2017 by a unanimous 8–0 decision, making her the first Korean president to be removed from office. On 6 April 2018, South Korean courts sentenced her to 24 years in prison (later increased to 25 years) for corruption and abuse of power. In 2018, two separate criminal cases increased her sentence by seven years: five years for illegally taking off-the-books funds from the National Intelligence Service (NIS) and two years for illegally interfering in the Saenuri Party primaries in the 2016 legislative election. On 24 December 2021, she was granted a pardon on compassionate grounds by President Moon Jae-in, was released from prison on 31 December, and returned home on 24 March 2022. Park chose not to vote in the 2017 South Korean presidential election.

Park advocated for ordinary people to organize a supplementary budget promptly for economic policy, jobs, and livelihoods, and encouraged the growth of the gig economy. On 8 April 2014, she signed the Australia–Korea Free Trade Agreement with Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott. She proposed eliminating the "Four Major Social Evils"—sexual violence, domestic violence, school violence, and unsafe food, noting that statistics indicated increases in sexual and domestic violence during that period, though without citing data, school violence and food safety remained significant public concerns. On 17 June, she launched the National Unity Committee, chaired by former Democratic United Party Advisor Han Kwang-ok, to advise on resolving societal conflicts and fostering co-existence and co-prosperity. After taking office, Park met with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and President Barack Obama; her first foreign trip, in May 2013, included visits to Washington, D.C., New York City, and Los Angeles. During summit talks at the White House, Park and Obama issued a joint declaration strengthening the American-South Korean alliance, discussed peace in Northeast Asia, and agreed on a joint statement for comprehensive energy cooperation and the establishment of a policy cooperation committee on information and communication technology. Park also urged the U.S. to expand the annual visa quota for South Korean professionals to boost economic cooperation. In June 2013, she visited China, meeting with President Xi Jinping, and on 13 November 2013, held an extended meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose visit was the first among leaders of the U.S., China, Japan, and Russia; the two leaders considered combining Korea's Eurasian Initiative with Russia's Asia-Pacific Policy and issued a joint communique and held a joint press conference. Earlier, at the September 2013 G-20 Summit in St. Petersburg, Park met Putin separately to discuss economic cooperation and North Korean issues, marking the first Korea–Russia summit since her inauguration. During her meeting with Russian Far East Minister Viktor Ishaev, she stated Russia was a key strategic partner. North Korea conducted provocations, including violating a UN Security Council resolution, firing a long-range missile on 12 December 2012, and carrying out a third nuclear test on 12 February 2013, nullifying non-aggression agreements on 8 March, and withdrawing workers from the Kaesong Industrial Region on 8 April. Park maintained that South Korea would not yield to North Korean provocations and would seek policy coordination with the U.S., China, and the UN, a stance that gained support from South Koreans and major powers and contributed to the unanimous adoption of UN Security Council Resolution 2094 on 7 March 2013. As a result, North Korea ceased provocations on 6 June and proposed discussions on reopening the Kaesong Industrial Complex. Park stated that peace and unification are the shared wish of all 70 million Koreans and that her administration would work to achieve this goal, emphasizing that reunification should improve quality of life, expand freedom and human rights, and build a prosperous peninsula. She also stated that North Korea must accept her trust-building policy initiative. Her policy on North Korea and unification is reflected in the Korean Peninsula Trust-building Process, with the Ministry of Unification announcing a vision of "realizing a new unified Korea that ensures everyone's happiness," including normalizing inter-Korean relations, launching small-scale unification projects, and strengthening unification capabilities. Park outlined a three-stage unification initiative: securing peace, achieving economic integration, and reaching political integration, with humanitarian assistance, inter-Korean exchanges, and the "Vision Korea project" to establish a single economic community, contingent on mutual trust and North Korean denuclearization. On 28 March 2014, during a state visit to Germany, she proposed three steps to North Korea, starting with jointly managing rivers and forests across the two Koreas, and urged North Korea to attend the UN Convention on Biological Diversity conference in Pyeongchang in October. In May 2014, Park warned that a new North Korean nuclear test could trigger a "nuclear domino effect," potentially prompting neighbors to acquire nuclear weapons. On 18 May 2014, she announced plans to dismantle the South Korean Coast Guard after its poor response during the MV Sewol ferry disaster, transferring investigation and information roles to the National Police and rescue and ocean security roles to the Department for National Safety, with the Korean Ministry of Security and Public Administration being newly established. On 19 November 2014, the Korea Coast Guard and National Emergency Management Agency ceased control as the Ministry of Public Safety and Security was founded. On 26 May 2015, Park urged the head of the Asian Development Bank to cooperate with South Korea and the China-led Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, following South Korea's official application to join the latter in late March 2015. On 1 May 2016, Park became the first South Korean president to visit Iran, leading a 236-member delegation of businessmen and entrepreneurs for a three-day visit to Tehran, where she met President Hassan Rouhani and Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and signed 19 basic agreements to expand cooperation. Iran's President Rouhani stated that bilateral trade would grow from $6 billion to $18 billion. In the 2016 general elections on 13 April, the Saenuri Party lost its majority and first-party status in the National Assembly, with Park criticized for her role in the election and nomination process, and pro-Park faction members blamed for the defeat. Park loyalists also performed poorly in constituency elections, hindering her proposed economic reforms and leading conservative The Chosun Ilbo to state that her "lame duck period" began earlier than any previous administration. In July 2013, public support for Park reached 63 percent, higher than her 52 percent election vote share, attributed to her principled North Korea policy, constructive outcomes from U.S. and Chinese visits, and distancing from internal disputes. By January 2015, her approval rating had dropped to 30 percent due to the MV Sewol sinking and North Korea disputes, rising to 54 percent by September 2015 due to successful diplomacy defusing a military standoff with North Korea, but falling to 31.5 percent after the 2016 election loss, a drop of 8.1 percentage points. On 4 November 2016, her ratings fell to 4–5% as details of her relationship with Choi Soon-sil were exposed in the 2016 South Korean political scandal. Park was arrested on 31 March 2017 and held at the Seoul Detention Center in Uiwang, Gyeonggi Province. On 17 April 2017, she was formally charged with abuse of power, bribery, coercion, and leaking government secrets, denying the charges during five rounds of interrogation. Prosecutors sought a 30-year prison term and a fine of ₩188.5 billion (US$110,579,397). On 6 April 2018, a three-judge panel of the Central District Court in Seoul sentenced her to 24 years in prison and a fine of ₩18 billion (US$16,798,683), finding her guilty of 16 out of 18 charges. In June 2018, three former NIS directors—Lee Byung-kee, Lee Byung-ho, and Nam Jae-joon—were found guilty of bribery for illegally transferring funds from the NIS budget to Park's office, which were then used for private purposes and bribes. On 24 August 2018, Park's sentence was increased to 25 years. In July 2020, an appellate court reduced her sentence to 20 years, citing that she received little personal benefit and was cleared of alleged extortion from conglomerates donating to Choi Soon-sil's foundations. In January 2021, South Korea's top court upheld the 20-year sentence. On 24 December 2021, Park was pardoned by President Moon Jae-in, citing her deteriorating health and the need to "overcome unfortunate past history and promote national unity." She was released from prison on 31 December and returned home on 24 March 2022. New President Yoon Suk-yeol invited her to his inauguration ceremony on 10 May 2022. Park faced criticism for being the "daughter of a dictator" (Park Chung Hee), with supporters of Lee Myung-bak criticizing her lack of support for his administration. A 2012 national-level poll found that 59% of respondents did not believe she was a "daughter of a dictator," while 36% did. Park Chung Hee's legacy became contested after the 1997 financial crisis, with GNP party elites promoting his economic achievements to reshape his image. In a 2012 interview with CJB, Park stated her father's 1961 May 16 coup was a "revolution to save the country," asserting that politicians should not debate whether it was a coup or revolution. A July 2012 survey found that 50% of respondents disagreed with her view that the coup was "unavoidable, the best possible choice, and advisable," while 37% agreed. Another survey showed 42% agreed it was unavoidable, while 46% disagreed. Because Park inherited strong regional and generational support from her father and his economic legacy, opponents used this to criticize her. Park faced scrutiny over the Jeongsoo Scholarship Foundation, formerly known as Buil (linked to the Busan Ilbo newspaper), which her father and she headed; original owners claimed they were forced to transfer it to her father. Liberty Korea Party member Nam Kyung-pil criticized the party's Park-centered nature, stating that repeated instances of Park giving press conferences before party meetings and having her statements adopted as official positions suggested democracy had disappeared. Critics also noted that Park's behavior in the 2012 election campaign was a mix of trend-following and corner-cutting, contrasting with her principled opposition to revising the Sejong City multifunctional administrative city plan. For example, Yim Tae-hee criticized Park for voting down a motion to arrest Chung Doo-un, a lawmaker implicated in bank bribery, and Ahn Sang-soo accused her of "saying one thing yesterday and another today." Park fired Yoon Chang-jung, a Blue House spokesman, after allegations from Washington Police that he committed sexual assault against an intern at the South Korean Embassy in Washington during her first U.S. visit. Just before the 2012 presidential election, the opposition alleged that NIS public servants organized an online campaign promoting Park and attacking opponents, a violation of the Korean Constitution. To prove the allegation, the opposition, along with police and the Central Election Assistance Commission, investigated. A 29-year-old female agent, Ha-Young Kim, who ran an illegal online campaign, locked herself in her home, leading to a three-day standoff that provoked political tension. The opposition accused the intelligence service of blocking the investigation, while Park and her party accused the opposition of harassing the agent. Later, during the presidential debate, Kim Yong-pan, then chief of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency, announced there was no evidence of illegal online postings from the agent's laptop, an announcement believed to have significantly affected the election outcome. After months of investigation, prosecutors concluded in mid-June 2013 that NIS chief Won Sei-hoon, who served under former President Lee Myung-bak, ordered agents to conduct a systematic online smear campaign against opposition candidates using hundreds of user IDs. The special investigation found that agents systematically intervened in domestic politics through thousands of cyber postings. Kim Yong-pan was prosecuted without physical detention on charges of abusing his authority to obstruct police investigations.

Park faced significant political and legal challenges throughout her presidency. In the lead-up to the presidential election, Park was criticized for allegedly harassing a woman during a presidential candidate debate, where she claimed the self-lock-in standoff violated a female right. Three days before the election, Kim Yong-pan, then chief of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency (SMPA), publicly stated there was no evidence of illegal online postings from a female agent’s laptop, an announcement that the opposing party believed significantly influenced the election outcome. Despite this, internal police CCTV recordings revealed that analysts had already identified illegal online postings targeting opposition candidates, suggesting intentional misinformation. The prosecution concluded in mid-June 2013 that Won Sei-hoon, former NIS chief under President Lee Myung-bak, ordered agents to conduct a systematic online smear campaign, resulting in 55,689 messages posted on Twitter over three months. The special investigation team, led by Yoon Suk-ryul, was disbanded, with Yoon returning to his original position as head of the Yeoju branch of the Supreme Prosecutors Office. Park also faced criticism for holding press conferences with pre-submitted questions and prepared answers, with opponents labeling her as "No communication" (Bultong). In November 2015, around 80,000 anti-government protesters clashed with security forces in Seoul, demanding her resignation over her business-friendly labor policies and the mandate for state-issued history textbooks in schools starting in 2017. Following the 2014 Sewol ferry disaster, the Park administration created a commission to monitor and prosecute social media critics, and Japanese journalist Tatsuya Kato was indicted for defamation after reporting on a relationship between Park and Choi Soon-sil’s husband, Chung Yoon-hoi. On 25 June 2015, Park made a statement criticizing Yu Seungmin of the Saenuri Party, which was criticized as an attempt to influence his election, though the National Election Commission ruled it did not violate the Public Official Election Act. In 2015, Park reached an agreement with Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe on the comfort women issue, including a $8.8 million assistance fund and a commitment to "irreversibly resolve" the matter, though President Moon Jae-in later terminated the deal in 2017. Investigations into Park’s relationship with Choi Soon-sil began in October 2016, revealing that Choi, without official government status, accessed confidential information and acted as a close confidant, extorting ₩77.4 billion (about $75 million) from chaebols and establishing two foundations, Mir and K-sports. Choi was also accused of influencing Ewha Womans University’s admission criteria for her daughter, Chung Yoo-ra, and of misusing a South Korean overseas development project in Myanmar for personal gain. Ahn Jong-bum and Jeong Ho-sung, top aides, were arrested for abuse of power and aiding Choi, denying wrongdoing and claiming they followed Park’s orders. On 25 October 2016, Park publicly acknowledged her close ties with Choi, and on 28 October, she dismissed key staff, causing her approval rating to plummet to 4%, with ratings as low as 1–3% among those under 60, the worst in Korean history. This triggered mass protests, including over 1 million participants at Gwanghwamun Square on 12 November and another 1 million on 19 November, demanding her resignation or impeachment. Park fired cabinet members and the prime minister, Hwang Kyo-ahn, with controversy arising over the claim that the dismissal was via text message. The Supreme Prosecutors' Office charged Park with collusion with Choi and two aides, marking the first time a serving South Korean president was questioned by prosecutors. Massive demonstrations began in early November 2016. On 29 November 2016, Park offered to resign and requested a transfer of power, but opposition parties rejected the offer, accusing her of evading impeachment. The National Assembly filed an impeachment motion on 9 December 2016, which passed with 234 votes, suspending Park’s presidential powers and transferring them to Hwang Kyo-ahn as acting president. On 10 March 2017, the Constitutional Court unanimously (8–0) upheld the impeachment, removing Park from office. On 26 March 2017, prosecutors sought an arrest warrant, which was granted by the Seoul Central District Court on 31 March 2017, leading to Park’s arrest and eventual sentencing to 25 years in prison. In December 2021, President Moon Jae-in granted Park a pardon to promote national reconciliation and address the national crisis from the COVID-19 pandemic, citing her declining health. The pardon was part of a broader amnesty that benefited 700 prisoners, reducing or eliminating their remaining sentences. Park returned home in March 2022 after being hospitalized at Samsung Medical Center.
